fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM from Recovery
fixSteps.instruction: In Recovery Command Prompt: DISM /Image:C:\ /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows.

fixSteps.title: Uninstall recent Windows update
fixSteps.instruction: From Recovery Environment: Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Uninstall Updates. Select the most recent quality or feature update.

fixSteps.title: Perform in-place repair install
fixSteps.instruction: If other methods fail, boot from Windows installation media. Choose Upgrade to repair Windows while keeping files and applications.

whenToCallPro: If system restore, SFC, and update removal all fail, a professional can perform manual service repair or a targeted repair installation.

faq.a: The BSOD may not identify the specific service. Check Event Viewer from Recovery Environment (if accessible) or analyze the crash dump.

faq.q: Can I fix this without reinstalling?
faq.a: Usually yes. System Restore, SFC/DISM, and update removal resolve most cases. A repair install is a last resort that preserves your files.
Your files are not affected by this service failure. They remain on disk. Even a repair install preserves personal files.

title: exFAT File System Error
shortDescription: A critical error occurred in the exFAT file system driver.
fullDescription:
The EXFAT_FILE_SYSTEM BSOD indicates that the exFAT file system driver encountered an unrecoverable error. exFAT is commonly used on USB flash drives, SD cards, and external drives for cross-platform compatibility.

The error typically occurs when accessing a corrupted exFAT volume, when the exFAT driver encounters an unexpected file system structure, or when the storage media has physical errors.

Formatting the affected drive or repairing file system errors usually resolves the issue.

causes.cause: Corrupted exFAT file system on removable media
Unsafe removal of USB drive during write
Physical errors on flash drive or SD card

symptoms: Crash when inserting USB drive or SD card
BSOD when browsing files on exFAT volume
Drive shows raw or unformatted in Disk Management
File system errors on the removable drive

fixSteps.title: Safely remove the device
fixSteps.instruction: If the system boots after the crash, do not immediately reinsert the drive. If it is inserted, use Safely Remove Hardware before removing it.

fixSteps.title: Check the drive on another computer
fixSteps.instruction: Insert the drive in another computer (or try a Linux live USB) to see if the file system is accessible. Back up any important files.

fixSteps.title: Run CHKDSK on the exFAT volume
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt. Run: chkdsk E: /f (replace E: with the drive letter). This repairs file system errors on the exFAT volume.

fixSteps.title: Format the drive
fixSteps.instruction: If CHKDSK cannot repair the drive, back up any recoverable data, then format the drive: right-click in File Explorer > Format > exFAT > Quick Format.

fixSteps.title: Update Windows
fixSteps.instruction: Install all pending Windows Updates to ensure you have the latest exFAT driver, which may contain bug fixes.

whenToCallPro: If important data on the drive cannot be accessed and CHKDSK fails, a data recovery professional may be able to retrieve files.

faq.a: exFAT is a file system designed for flash drives and SD cards. It supports files larger than 4GB (unlike FAT32) and works on both Windows and macOS.

faq.q: Why did my USB drive cause a BSOD?
faq.a: A corrupted file system on the USB drive can crash the exFAT driver when Windows tries to read it. Always use Safely Remove Hardware before unplugging drives.

faq.q: Should I use NTFS instead of exFAT?
faq.a: If the drive is only used with Windows, NTFS is more reliable. Use exFAT only when cross-platform compatibility (Windows + macOS) is needed.

title: I/O Subsystem Initialization Failed
shortDescription: The I/O subsystem failed to initialize during Windows boot.
fullDescription:
The IO1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED BSOD occurs when the Windows I/O subsystem fails during the early boot initialization phase. The I/O subsystem is fundamental to Windows — it handles all input/output operations including disk access, network communication, and device management.

This error typically indicates severe system file corruption, missing critical drivers, or hardware issues preventing the I/O subsystem from starting. It can also occur after an interrupted Windows update.

Recovery requires booting from external media and repairing the Windows installation.
symptoms: Blue screen with IO1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED during boot
Error appears after interrupted update or power loss during boot

fixSteps.title: Boot to Recovery Environment
fixSteps.instruction: Boot from Windows installation media or recovery drive. Select Repair your computer > Troubleshoot > Advanced Options.

fixSteps.title: Run Startup Repair
fixSteps.instruction: From Advanced Options, select Startup Repair. Let it attempt automatic repair of boot components.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM offline
fixSteps.instruction: From Recovery Command Prompt: DISM /Image:C:\ /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows.

fixSteps.title: Perform repair install
fixSteps.instruction: If SFC/DISM cannot fix the issue, use the Windows installation media to perform a repair install (upgrade) that replaces system files while keeping data.

whenToCallPro: If Startup Repair and SFC fail, and a repair install is not successful, a professional can determine if the issue is hardware-related.

faq.q: What caused the I/O initialization to fail?
faq.a: Usually corrupted system files from a failed update, power loss during boot, or disk errors. The I/O subsystem needs intact system files to start.
Yes. Your personal files are likely intact on the disk. Boot from a Linux live USB or connect the drive to another computer to access files.

faq.q: Will a repair install lose my programs?
faq.a: A repair install (in-place upgrade) preserves your files, settings, and installed applications. It only replaces Windows system files.

title: No Pages Available
shortDescription: The system ran out of memory pages, unable to allocate any more physical memory.
fullDescription:
The NO_PAGES_AVAILABLE BSOD occurs when Windows completely exhausts all available memory pages. This means there is no physical memory or page file space left for the system to allocate.

This error is different from the STATUS_NO_MEMORY error — it occurs at a lower level when the memory manager cannot find any free pages at all. It is typically caused by massive memory leaks in drivers, insufficient RAM combined with heavy workloads, or a disabled/full page file.

Increasing available memory and fixing memory leaks are the primary solutions.

causes.cause: Page file disabled or on a full disk

symptoms: System becomes extremely slow before crash
Applications stop responding and show not responding
Disk usage at 100% from heavy paging
Task Manager shows near 100% memory usage

fixSteps.title: Check and configure page file
fixSteps.instruction: Go to System Properties > Advanced > Performance Settings > Advanced > Virtual Memory. Ensure page file is enabled and set to at least 1.5x RAM on a drive with free space.

fixSteps.title: Identify memory-consuming processes
fixSteps.instruction: Open Task Manager, sort by Memory. Look for processes using excessive memory. Also check non-paged and paged pool sizes in the Performance > Memory section.

fixSteps.title: Update drivers to fix memory leaks
fixSteps.instruction: Update all drivers, especially network, storage, and GPU drivers. Use RAMMap or poolmon to identify which pool tag is consuming the most memory.

fixSteps.title: Add more RAM
fixSteps.instruction: If your system regularly uses over 80% of RAM, consider upgrading. Check your motherboard specs for maximum supported RAM and compatible module types.

whenToCallPro: If you cannot identify the source of memory consumption or if a kernel memory leak requires dump analysis to trace.

faq.q: How is this different from STATUS_NO_MEMORY?
faq.a: NO_PAGES_AVAILABLE is a lower-level error from the memory manager itself, while STATUS_NO_MEMORY is returned to callers that request memory. Both indicate memory exhaustion.

faq.q: Will adding RAM fix this permanently?
faq.a: If the cause is a memory leak, adding RAM only delays the crash. The leak must be fixed by updating the responsible driver or software.

faq.q: Can I tell which driver is leaking memory?
faq.a: Use RAMMap or poolmon.exe to see pool memory usage by tag. Each pool tag identifies which driver made the allocation.

title: Process Initialization Failed
shortDescription: A critical process failed during its initialization phase.
fullDescription:
The PROCESS_INITIALIZATION_FAILED BSOD occurs when a system-critical process cannot complete its initialization. This is similar to CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED but occurs specifically during the initialization phase rather than during runtime.

The error indicates that Windows system files required for process initialization are missing, corrupted, or inaccessible. This can happen after a bad update, disk corruption, or system file modification.

System file repair or Windows reinstallation is typically required.
symptoms: Error appears after update or system change

fixSteps.title: Try System Restore
fixSteps.instruction: Boot from Recovery Environment. Use System Restore to return to a point before the error appeared.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM offline
fixSteps.instruction: From Recovery Command Prompt: DISM /Image:C:\ /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth then sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows.

fixSteps.title: Check disk integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Run chkdsk C: /f /r from Recovery Command Prompt to repair disk errors that may have corrupted system files.

fixSteps.title: Repair install Windows
fixSteps.instruction: Boot from Windows installation media and select Upgrade to perform an in-place repair that replaces system files.

whenToCallPro: If System Restore, SFC, and repair install all fail, professional data recovery and OS reinstallation may be needed.

faq.q: Can I fix this without losing data?
faq.a: Yes. System Restore, SFC, and repair install all preserve your personal files. Only a clean install would remove them (and you can still back up first).

faq.q: Why did this happen after an update?
faq.a: Windows updates replace system files. If the update was interrupted or a file was corrupted during the process, initialization can fail.
While malware can cause this by modifying system files, it is more commonly caused by update failures or disk errors. Scan with Windows Defender Offline from the Recovery Environment.

title: Phase 1 Initialization Failed
shortDescription: Windows kernel failed during phase 1 of system initialization.
fullDescription:
The PHASE1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED BSOD occurs during the first phase of Windows kernel initialization. This is very early in the boot process, where the kernel sets up fundamental data structures, initializes the memory manager, and prepares the system for driver loading.

This error indicates a severe problem with the Windows installation, boot configuration, or hardware compatibility. It is often caused by corrupt system files, incompatible hardware after a motherboard swap, or BIOS/UEFI issues.

Recovery may require a repair installation or clean Windows install.
symptoms: Blue screen with PHASE1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED very early in boot
System never reaches the Windows logo screen
Cannot access Safe Mode or Recovery

fixSteps.title: Reset BIOS to defaults
fixSteps.instruction: Enter BIOS/UEFI and load default settings. Ensure the correct boot device is selected and Secure Boot/CSM settings are appropriate.

fixSteps.title: Boot from recovery media
fixSteps.instruction: Create Windows installation USB on another computer. Boot from it and try Startup Repair from Troubleshoot > Advanced Options.

fixSteps.title: Run offline SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: From Recovery Command Prompt: DISM /Image:C:\ /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows.

fixSteps.title: Perform clean or repair install
fixSteps.instruction: If the above fails, attempt a repair install first (preserves data). If that fails, perform a clean install after backing up data via Linux live USB.

whenToCallPro: If you need to recover data from the drive before reinstalling, or if the error occurs on new hardware and you suspect compatibility issues.

faq.q: Why does this happen so early in boot?
faq.a: Phase 1 initialization is one of the earliest boot stages. Problems here usually mean fundamental system files are missing or the hardware configuration has changed dramatically.
Yes. Boot from a Linux live USB or connect the drive to another computer to copy your files before reinstalling Windows.
Not necessarily. This is more often a software/configuration issue. Test with a fresh Windows install to rule out hardware problems.

title: Internal Power Error
shortDescription: The power management subsystem encountered a fatal error.
fullDescription:
The INTERNAL_POWER_ERROR BSOD indicates a fatal error in the Windows power management subsystem. This subsystem handles sleep, hibernate, power state transitions, and battery management.

The error commonly occurs during sleep or hibernate transitions, when waking from sleep, or during shutdown. Incompatible drivers, particularly GPU and storage drivers, that do not properly handle power state changes are the most frequent cause.

This error is especially common on laptops where power management is more complex than on desktops.

causes.cause: Driver not handling power state transition correctly
Outdated GPU driver with sleep/wake bugs
Insufficient disk space for hibernate file

symptoms: Crash when putting system to sleep or hibernating

fixSteps.title: Disable hibernate and re-enable
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt. Run: powercfg /hibernate off then powercfg /hibernate on. This recreates the hibernate file.

fixSteps.title: Update GPU and chipset drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Download and install the latest GPU driver from NVIDIA/AMD/Intel. Also update the chipset driver from the motherboard/laptop manufacturer.

fixSteps.title: Run power troubleshooter
fixSteps.instruction: Go to Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Power. Run the troubleshooter and apply suggested fixes.

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS
fixSteps.instruction: Check your laptop/motherboard manufacturer for BIOS updates that address power management issues.

fixSteps.title: Disable hybrid sleep
fixSteps.instruction: Go to Control Panel > Power Options > Change plan settings > Change advanced. Under Sleep > Allow hybrid sleep, set to Off.

whenToCallPro: If the error persists after driver updates and BIOS update, or if the laptop has complex docking station or multi-monitor power management issues.

faq.a: As a workaround, you can disable sleep and use shutdown instead. But the real fix is updating drivers and BIOS to properly handle power states.

faq.q: Why does this happen on laptops more than desktops?
faq.a: Laptops have more complex power management including battery, lid close actions, multiple power plans, and connected standby. More complexity means more potential for driver issues.
Yes, hibernate is safe when drivers properly support it. If you experience crashes during hibernate, disable it as a workaround while updating drivers.

title: Unhandled Kernel-Mode Exception
shortDescription: A kernel-mode program generated an exception that the error handler did not catch.
fullDescription:
This stop code means a kernel-mode program generated an exception which the error handler did not catch. It is a general-purpose kernel error typically caused by faulty drivers, defective RAM, corrupted system files, or aggressive overclocking.

The second parameter in the bug check indicates the type of exception (e.g., 0xC0000005 is an access violation). The third parameter gives the address where the exception occurred, which WinDbg can resolve to a specific driver.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If memory tests fail or WinDbg points to a signed Microsoft driver you cannot replace, a technician can reinstall Windows cleanly or test hardware.

faq.a: 0xC0000005 is STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION, meaning a kernel routine tried to read or write invalid memory.

faq.q: Is this fixable without reinstalling Windows?
faq.a: Usually yes. Updating drivers, running SFC, and testing RAM resolve most cases.
Sometimes. Cumulative updates ship fixes for common kernel bugs; keep Windows current.

title: Driver Verifier Flagged a Driver Violation
shortDescription: Driver Verifier detected a driver that violated one of the rules it was monitoring.
fullDescription:
This stop code is intentionally triggered when Driver Verifier is enabled and it catches a misbehaving kernel driver. Verifier subjects drivers to stricter rules (special pool checks, IRQL checks, I/O verification) than normal runtime and deliberately bugchecks on the first violation.

If you did not enable Verifier yourself, another user or a troubleshooting guide may have. Disabling Verifier stops the BSODs but does not fix the underlying driver bug.

causes.cause: Buggy third-party kernel driver under Verifier stress
Outdated driver incompatible with current Windows

symptoms: System boots normally in Safe Mode
Second parameter identifies the violation type

fixSteps.title: Disable Driver Verifier
fixSteps.instruction: Boot into Safe Mode, open Command Prompt as admin, and run: verifier /reset. Reboot the PC.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Re-run Verifier on suspect drivers only
fixSteps.instruction: Run verifier.exe, choose Create custom settings, and select only the driver(s) you suspect. This isolates the faulty module.

whenToCallPro: If Verifier consistently flags a signed vendor driver, contact the vendor or engage a Windows expert to interpret the violation parameters.

faq.q: I didn't enable Verifier, why is it running?
faq.a: Another user, a tech support session, or a registry tweak may have enabled it. Run verifier /reset to disable.

faq.q: Is the flagged driver really broken?
faq.a: Almost always yes. Verifier uses tight but valid rules; violations indicate real bugs even if they rarely trigger in normal use.

faq.q: Will disabling Verifier cause data loss?
faq.a: No. Verifier only monitors drivers; disabling it returns Windows to normal operation.

title: Driver Corrupted the Executive Pool
shortDescription: A driver attempted to access an invalid memory address at a raised IRQL, corrupting the executive pool.
fullDescription:
This bug check indicates a kernel-mode driver wrote to an invalid location in the system executive (paged or non-paged) pool. Pool corruption is almost always caused by a defective driver, though faulty RAM can produce similar symptoms.

Use Driver Verifier with Special Pool enabled on suspect drivers to catch the offender on the first invalid write instead of at a random later time.

causes.cause: Faulty kernel-mode driver corrupting pool memory

symptoms: Different modules named in each dump

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

fixSteps.title: Enable Driver Verifier with Special Pool
fixSteps.instruction: Run verifier.exe, select Create standard settings, and monitor non-Microsoft drivers. Special Pool will catch pool overruns immediately.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If Verifier and MemTest86 both clear and the problem persists, escalate to a technician with WinDbg experience to trace the pool corruption.

faq.a: It is the kernel's main heap for dynamic allocations used by drivers and kernel components.
Yes. A bit flip in pool memory looks identical to a driver overwrite. Always test RAM before replacing drivers.

faq.q: Is it safe to keep using the PC?
faq.a: No. Pool corruption can silently damage files; stop using the machine until the root cause is fixed.

title: Generic File System Error
shortDescription: An unexpected error occurred inside a Windows file-system driver.
fullDescription:
This bug check indicates an unspecified error from the file-system layer, typically when none of the more specific NTFS, FAT, or ReFS codes apply. It is often caused by disk corruption, third-party filter drivers (antivirus, backup, encryption), or a failing drive.

Because the error is generic, analyzing the minidump in WinDbg to identify the calling driver is the fastest way to narrow down the cause.

causes.cause: Corrupted file-system metadata on the drive
Bad system RAM corrupting file-system structures

symptoms: Crash during file copy or backup
Event Viewer logs disk errors before the crash

fixSteps.title: Check disk integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: chkdsk C: /f /r. Allow the scan to run on next reboot.

fixSteps.title: Temporarily uninstall file-system filter drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Uninstall third-party antivirus, backup agents, and disk encryption tools one at a time and test for stability.

fixSteps.title: Check drive SMART status
fixSteps.instruction: Install CrystalDiskInfo and verify reallocated sectors, pending sectors, and uncorrectable errors are at zero.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If SMART warns of drive failure or CHKDSK cannot complete, call a data-recovery professional before further writes compound the damage.

faq.q: Does this always mean a failing drive?
faq.a: No, but drive health should be checked first because a failing disk is the most serious cause.
Yes. File-system filter drivers from security tools frequently cause this error after updates.
Back up immediately. File-system BSODs sometimes accompany metadata corruption that can spread if ignored.

title: Thread Exited While Still Owning a Mutex
shortDescription: A thread is exiting while it still owns a mutex, which would leave the mutex permanently locked.
fullDescription:
This rare bug check occurs when a kernel thread terminates without releasing a mutex it acquired. Because other threads could block on the orphaned mutex forever, Windows halts the system instead of continuing in an undefined state.

It is almost always a kernel driver bug. The responsible driver is identified by the second parameter of the bug check and in the minidump.

causes.cause: Buggy third-party anti-cheat or security driver

symptoms: Crash during shutdown or driver unload
Rare, usually reproducible on a specific workload

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Uninstall anti-cheat or security drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Temporarily remove Faceit AC, EasyAntiCheat, Riot Vanguard, or similar tools to test whether they are responsible.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

whenToCallPro: This is a driver synchronization bug. If updating the responsible driver does not fix it, contact the vendor with the minidump.

faq.q: Can I fix the driver myself?
faq.a: No. You must rely on the driver vendor to ship a corrected version.

faq.q: Will a Windows reinstall fix this?
faq.a: Only if the faulty driver is replaced. A clean install with the same driver will show the same BSOD.

title: Unhandled Exception in an Interrupt Handler
shortDescription: An exception occurred inside an interrupt service routine and was not handled.
fullDescription:
This bug check means the CPU raised an exception (such as an access violation or divide-by-zero) while executing an interrupt service routine, and the ISR did not handle it. ISRs run at high IRQL where unhandled exceptions cannot be recovered.

The root cause is almost always a defective hardware device or its driver. It can also be triggered by unstable overclocking that causes the CPU to fault during normal interrupts.

causes.cause: Buggy driver for a hardware device
Failing CPU, chipset, or PCIe device

symptoms: Crash during high interrupt load (network, audio)

fixSteps.title: Revert overclocking
fixSteps.instruction: Enter BIOS/UEFI and load optimized defaults. Retest for stability before re-enabling XMP/DOCP.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Isolate failing hardware
fixSteps.instruction: Unplug non-essential PCIe cards and USB devices one at a time to identify the culprit.

whenToCallPro: If the crash persists at default BIOS settings with no add-in cards, the motherboard or CPU may be failing and should be evaluated by a technician.

faq.a: Frequently yes, especially if multiple drivers are named across dumps.
Yes. Enabling XMP/DOCP raises the memory controller load; disable it to test.

title: Windows Hardware Error Architecture Logger Failed to Start
shortDescription: The WHEA error logger could not initialize during Windows startup.
fullDescription:
This bug check occurs early in boot when the Windows Hardware Error Architecture (WHEA) subsystem cannot start. Because WHEA is required for reporting machine-check exceptions, Windows refuses to continue without it.

The usual cause is a corrupt or incompatible BIOS/UEFI firmware, an ACPI table issue, or a hardware fault in the CPU or chipset. A BIOS update frequently resolves the issue.

causes.cause: ACPI table bug on specific motherboards

symptoms: System cannot reach the Windows login screen

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS/UEFI
fixSteps.instruction: Download the latest BIOS from the motherboard manufacturer and flash it per their instructions. Do not interrupt the update.

fixSteps.title: Clear CMOS
fixSteps.instruction: Power off, unplug, remove the CMOS battery for 30 seconds, then reinsert. Alternatively use the motherboard clear-CMOS jumper.

fixSteps.title: Load BIOS defaults
fixSteps.instruction: Enter BIOS setup and select Load Optimized Defaults. Save and reboot.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: If BIOS updates and CMOS resets do not help, the motherboard or CPU may be at fault and require professional diagnosis.

faq.a: Possibly, but try a BIOS update first as firmware bugs are far more common than CPU failure.
No. WHEA is required in modern Windows and cannot be safely disabled.

title: Kernel-Mode Manager Rule Violation
shortDescription: A kernel-mode manager detected a violation of its invariants and halted the system.
fullDescription:
This bug check is raised when a kernel subsystem manager detects a rule violation (for example, an illegal state transition or an invalid handle). It most often appears on systems with outdated or incompatible drivers, particularly after a Windows feature update.

The parameters in the bugcheck identify which manager detected the issue. Analyzing the crash dump in WinDbg is the most reliable way to pinpoint the responsible module.

causes.cause: Incompatible driver after Windows feature update

symptoms: Started after a Windows feature update

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Roll back a problematic Windows update
fixSteps.instruction: Go to Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates, then remove the most recent update and reboot.

whenToCallPro: If neither driver updates nor SFC fix the issue, a professional can analyze the minidump and identify the violating manager.

faq.q: Is this the same as KMODE_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED?
faq.a: No. The exception variant is a CPU fault; the manager-violation variant is Windows detecting an invalid kernel state.
It helps diagnose: if Safe Mode is stable, a third-party driver is the likely culprit.

title: Driver Accessed Memory After Freeing It
shortDescription: A driver attempted to read memory in special pool after the allocation was freed.
fullDescription:
This bug check is produced by Driver Verifier's Special Pool feature. When enabled, Verifier places each pool allocation on its own guard page and marks freed pages as no-access. Any read of freed memory triggers this immediate BSOD, making it easy to identify the offending driver.

It is almost never seen with Verifier off. If you see it spontaneously, check whether Verifier was enabled.

causes.cause: Use-after-free bug in a kernel driver
Driver Verifier left enabled after troubleshooting

symptoms: Occurs only when Driver Verifier is active
The faulting address is consistently in special pool range

fixSteps.title: Disable Driver Verifier
fixSteps.instruction: Open an admin Command Prompt and run: verifier /reset. Reboot.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Report the bug to the driver vendor
fixSteps.instruction: Capture the minidump and WinDbg !analyze -v output and send it to the driver vendor with reproduction steps.

whenToCallPro: Use-after-free bugs require the driver vendor to ship a patch; a technician can only help disable the affected driver in the meantime.

faq.q: Is this error dangerous without Verifier?
faq.a: Yes. Without Verifier the bug still exists but manifests as subtler random crashes.
Only by disabling Verifier. The underlying driver defect remains.

title: CPU Trap With No Identified Cause
shortDescription: An unknown CPU trap was raised that Windows could not classify.
fullDescription:
This bug check indicates that the CPU raised a trap (an exception or interrupt) whose origin Windows cannot determine. Because Windows cannot safely recover without knowing the cause, it halts.

TRAP_CAUSE_UNKNOWN almost always indicates a hardware problem: failing RAM, a dying CPU, or unstable overclock. Driver bugs can produce it but are less common.
symptoms: Crashes under load or at random
System unstable even at BIOS defaults

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

fixSteps.title: Reset BIOS to defaults
fixSteps.instruction: Load optimized defaults in BIOS and disable XMP/DOCP. Retest for stability.

fixSteps.title: Stress test the CPU
fixSteps.instruction: Run Prime95 Small FFTs for 30 minutes while monitoring temperatures with HWInfo64.

fixSteps.title: Check PSU and cables
fixSteps.instruction: Reseat all power connectors. If possible, swap in a known-good PSU to rule out dirty power.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If stress tests, memory tests, or BIOS resets do not stabilize the system, a technician should test hardware with known-good replacements.

faq.a: Usually, but a low-level driver bug can occasionally cause it. Test hardware first.
Yes. Aggressive CPU or RAM overclocks are a common trigger.

title: Driver Failed to Unlock Pages
shortDescription: A driver called MmProbeAndLockPages but failed to unlock them before completing an I/O request.
fullDescription:
This bug check is raised by Driver Verifier when a driver unmaps or completes an I/O request while still holding a lock on pages it acquired with MmProbeAndLockPages. Leaving pages locked would prevent them from being paged out and slowly exhaust memory.

The bug is in the driver code path and can only be fixed by the driver vendor. The dump file identifies the responsible driver.
symptoms: BSOD with DRIVER_LEFT_LOCKED_PAGES_IN_PROCESS when Verifier is enabled

fixSteps.title: Disable Driver Verifier
fixSteps.instruction: Run: verifier /reset in an admin Command Prompt and reboot.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Remove or replace the offending driver
fixSteps.instruction: Once identified, uninstall the driver or replace it with a version known to fix the leak.

whenToCallPro: Only the driver vendor can ship a proper fix. A technician can help identify the driver and remove it pending an update.

faq.a: Effectively yes. Locked pages cannot be reclaimed until the process exits.

faq.q: Does this happen with Verifier off?
faq.a: The bug still exists but only manifests as gradual memory pressure rather than a BSOD.

title: Process Terminated With Locked Pages
shortDescription: A process was terminated while it still had pages locked by a driver.
fullDescription:
This bug check fires when a process exits while a driver still holds locks on the process's memory pages. It usually accompanies DRIVER_LEFT_LOCKED_PAGES_IN_PROCESS and points at the same underlying driver defect.

The first parameter gives the number of locked pages, and WinDbg can identify the driver that owns the locks via the tracking database.

causes.cause: Driver failing to release page locks

symptoms: Crash when a specific application closes

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Disable Verifier
fixSteps.instruction: Run verifier /reset in an admin Command Prompt and reboot.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

whenToCallPro: Resolution depends on the driver vendor. A technician can help remove the problematic driver until a fix is released.

faq.q: Is the crashing app to blame?
faq.a: No. The process merely exposed the driver bug by exiting.

title: Invalid Kernel Executive Handle
shortDescription: The kernel executive attempted to manipulate a handle whose internal state was invalid.
fullDescription:
This bug check indicates that the kernel's handle table manager found a handle with corrupt reference counts or an impossible state. It typically results from kernel memory corruption caused by a faulty driver, RAM defects, or overrun pool buffers.

Because the corruption could spread silently, Windows halts immediately.

causes.cause: Kernel pool corruption by a driver

symptoms: Preceded by other pool or memory errors

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

whenToCallPro: If Verifier flags a specific driver, contact the vendor. If RAM tests fail, replace the modules.

faq.a: Yes. Stop using the PC until the corruption source is identified.

title: Registry Filter Driver Threw Unhandled Exception
shortDescription: A registry filter driver raised an unhandled exception during a registry operation.
fullDescription:
Windows allows drivers to filter registry calls (for example, security products monitor key writes). This bug check means such a filter driver encountered an exception it did not handle. The dump identifies the responsible driver.

Removing or updating the filter driver, usually part of antivirus or endpoint security software, resolves the crash.

causes.cause: Faulty antivirus or EDR registry filter
Outdated security product incompatible with current Windows

symptoms: Named driver belongs to a security product

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Uninstall security software
fixSteps.instruction: Remove third-party antivirus and re-test with Windows Defender only. Use the vendor's official removal tool if the uninstaller leaves drivers behind.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: If the faulting driver cannot be removed from Safe Mode, professional assistance may be needed to extract it manually.

faq.a: The version you are running has a bug. Updating to the current release usually fixes it.

faq.q: Can I keep using a registry cleaner?
faq.a: Most registry cleaners are unsafe and provide no performance benefit; uninstalling is recommended.

title: Thread Exited With Pending APC
shortDescription: A thread terminated while it still had an asynchronous procedure call (APC) pending.
fullDescription:
This bug check occurs when a thread exits the kernel with an APC still queued, meaning a driver queued work that was never delivered. The situation is a driver synchronization bug.

The second parameter is the address of the APC, which WinDbg can resolve to identify the driver that queued it.

causes.cause: Kernel driver with APC lifecycle bug
Outdated storage, network, or filter driver

symptoms: Occurs during shutdown or driver unload

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: The faulting driver must be updated or removed; contact the vendor with the WinDbg output if no update is available.

faq.a: No. APC leaks indicate real driver bugs that can destabilize the system further.

title: System Service Called at Raised IRQL
shortDescription: A user-mode thread returned to user mode while still at an elevated IRQL.
fullDescription:
This bug check indicates that kernel code forgot to lower the IRQL before returning to user mode. User mode is required to run at IRQL 0 (PASSIVE_LEVEL); raising it causes undefined behavior and Windows halts to prevent it.

The cause is always a kernel driver bug that raises IRQL but fails to lower it on every code path.
symptoms: Rare, typically reproducible under specific workloads

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: Only the driver vendor can ship a fix. A technician can help identify the culprit and disable it as a workaround.

faq.a: Only by removing the faulty driver; the code bug itself must be fixed by the vendor.

title: Third Session Initialization Failure
shortDescription: Windows failed to initialize session 3 during startup.
fullDescription:
This boot-time bug check indicates that session initialization failed. It often results from missing or corrupt session-manager components (smss.exe, win32k.sys) or from hardware/driver issues that prevent the session from loading graphical subsystems.

Recovery usually requires Startup Repair, a DISM offline repair, or a rollback to a known-good restore point.
symptoms: Boots briefly past the logo then crashes
Started after update or power loss

fixSteps.title: Run Startup Repair
fixSteps.instruction: Boot from Windows installation media, choose Repair your computer > Troubleshoot > Startup Repair.

fixSteps.title: Offline DISM repair
fixSteps.instruction: From the Windows recovery Command Prompt run: DISM /Image:C:\ /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth /Source:D:\sources\install.wim

fixSteps.title: System Restore from WinRE
fixSteps.instruction: Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > System Restore and pick a point before the issue.

fixSteps.title: Check disk integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: chkdsk C: /f /r. Allow the scan to run on next reboot.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If the machine cannot reach recovery or repair media fails, a technician can mount the disk offline and repair the boot files.

faq.a: Startup Repair and DISM do not touch user data; keep a backup anyway.

title: Second Session Initialization Failure
shortDescription: Windows failed to initialize session 2 during startup.
fullDescription: This bug check is raised when the second session fails to start during boot, commonly because of corrupt system components, a recent incompatible update, or disk errors. It typically appears alongside SESSION1/SESSION3 variants and responds to the same recovery steps.

fixSteps.title: Run Startup Repair
fixSteps.instruction: Boot recovery media and run Startup Repair.

fixSteps.title: Check disk integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: chkdsk C: /f /r. Allow the scan to run on next reboot.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Roll back recent update
fixSteps.instruction: In WinRE choose Uninstall updates and remove the most recent quality or feature update.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If recovery tools do not resolve the boot failure, a technician can perform an in-place repair install.

faq.a: Usually yes; these repair steps preserve user data.

title: First Session Initialization Failure
shortDescription: Windows failed to initialize session 1 during startup.
fullDescription: Session 1 is one of the earliest sessions established by the Session Manager. A failure here usually means corrupt system files or a driver that cannot load at this early stage. Recovery requires Windows installation media or a prior System Restore point.

fixSteps.title: Startup Repair
fixSteps.instruction: Use Windows recovery media to run Startup Repair.

fixSteps.title: Boot last known good via bcdedit
fixSteps.instruction: In Recovery Command Prompt: bcdedit /set {default} safeboot minimal, reboot to Safe Mode, then undo with bcdedit /deletevalue {default} safeboot.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Check disk integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: chkdsk C: /f /r. Allow the scan to run on next reboot.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If Startup Repair and offline DISM fail, an in-place upgrade reinstall is usually the next step.

faq.a: Not immediately. Startup Repair and offline DISM resolve most cases.

title: Critical User-Mode Subsystem Terminated
shortDescription: A user-mode subsystem such as csrss.exe or winlogon.exe failed, causing Windows to halt.
fullDescription:
This error (sometimes shown as WINLOGON_FATAL_ERROR) means a critical Windows user-mode subsystem terminated unexpectedly. Because these processes are required for Windows to run, the OS triggers a stop.

It is commonly caused by corrupt system files, failed Windows updates, or third-party software tampering with winlogon/csrss. System Restore and SFC/DISM resolve most cases.

fixSteps.title: System Restore from WinRE
fixSteps.instruction: Boot into Advanced Startup > Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > System Restore and select a pre-issue point.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Uninstall latest update from WinRE
fixSteps.instruction: Advanced Startup > Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Uninstall Updates > Uninstall latest quality update.

fixSteps.title: Full malware scan
fixSteps.instruction: Boot to Safe Mode with Networking and run Windows Defender Offline scan.

fixSteps.title: Check disk integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: chkdsk C: /f /r. Allow the scan to run on next reboot.

whenToCallPro: If repair tools cannot restore login, a technician can perform an in-place reinstall preserving data.

faq.a: Usually no. Repair options preserve user data.

faq.q: Can a Windows update cause it?
faq.a: Yes. This is a classic post-update failure signature.

title: Resilient File System Error
shortDescription: An error occurred inside the ReFS file-system driver.
fullDescription:
This bug check comes from the ReFS (Resilient File System) driver, used for Storage Spaces and some server workloads. Causes range from metadata corruption, underlying storage failures, to bugs in the ReFS driver itself.

ReFS is designed to be self-healing, but certain corruption patterns still trigger bugchecks. Checking the underlying disks and Storage Spaces health is the first step.

causes.cause: Underlying disk or Storage Spaces degradation
Buggy filter driver on ReFS volume

fixSteps.title: Check Storage Spaces health
fixSteps.instruction: Open PowerShell as admin and run: Get-VirtualDisk; Get-PhysicalDisk. Replace any failed drives.

fixSteps.title: Repair ReFS volume
fixSteps.instruction: Run: Repair-FileIntegrity -FileName X:\ in PowerShell. Allow it to complete.

fixSteps.title: Check disk SMART
fixSteps.instruction: Run CrystalDiskInfo to verify all drives in the pool are healthy.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: ReFS data recovery is specialized. If the volume mounts read-only or integrity repair fails, engage a data-recovery professional.

faq.q: Is ReFS less reliable than NTFS?
faq.a: No, but it is used in more complex Storage Spaces configurations where underlying failures are more consequential.

faq.q: Can I convert ReFS to NTFS?
faq.a: Not in place. You must back up data and reformat.

title: Stack Unwind on Corrupt Stack
shortDescription: Windows attempted to unwind a thread's stack but the stack was invalid.
fullDescription:
This bug check occurs during structured-exception unwinding when the stack walker detects that the stack pointer or frame data are corrupt. Stack corruption is typically caused by kernel drivers writing past buffer boundaries or by failing RAM.

Enabling Driver Verifier on non-Microsoft drivers helps pinpoint the offender.

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Enable Driver Verifier
fixSteps.instruction: Run verifier.exe, create standard settings for non-Microsoft drivers.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: If MemTest86 and Verifier both clear, a technician can check the CPU and motherboard for faults.

faq.a: Both are possible; test RAM first because it's faster.

title: Kernel Storage Slot Already Occupied
shortDescription: A driver tried to use a kernel storage slot that was already in use.
fullDescription:
This bug check is raised by newer Windows kernels when a driver tries to acquire a kernel TLS slot that is already owned. It is almost always a driver defect introduced during Windows 10/11 development.

Updating drivers and applying Windows cumulative updates resolves most cases.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Install pending Windows updates
fixSteps.instruction: Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates and install all pending items.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

whenToCallPro: If a third-party driver keeps triggering it even after updating, a technician can help remove the driver until a fix is released.

faq.a: Yes, it was introduced with newer Windows kernels for TLS-slot management.

title: Thread Terminated With Held Auto-Boost Lock
shortDescription: A thread was terminated while still holding a kernel auto-boost lock entry.
fullDescription:
This bug check is a stricter sibling of KERNEL_AUTO_BOOST_LOCK_ACQUISITION_WITH_RAISED_IRQL. It indicates a driver released a thread without unwinding a lock tracked by the auto-boost subsystem.

The minidump names the driver that acquired the lock; vendors must fix the driver.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: Driver vendor must issue a patch; meanwhile remove the driver if possible.

faq.q: Can I clear the leak myself?
faq.a: No, only a driver update fixes it.

title: Plug and Play Manager Detected Fatal Error
shortDescription: The Plug and Play manager encountered an unrecoverable error from a PnP driver.
fullDescription:
This bug check means a PnP driver returned an unexpected status or violated the PnP contract. Common triggers include incompatible storage controllers, network adapters, or USB hubs, especially after BIOS or Windows updates.

Safe Mode usually loads without the offending device, letting you update or roll back the PnP driver responsible.
symptoms: Occurs when a device is connected/disconnected

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS
fixSteps.instruction: Flash the latest motherboard firmware per OEM instructions.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Disconnect suspect hardware
fixSteps.instruction: Unplug non-essential USB/PCIe devices and test one at a time to identify the faulty unit.

whenToCallPro: If the crash persists with minimal hardware, a technician should test components.

faq.q: Could a USB device cause this?
faq.a: Yes; bad USB drivers and hubs are frequent causes.

title: Driver Failed to Respond to PnP Request
shortDescription: A driver did not complete a Plug and Play request within the watchdog timeout.
fullDescription:
The PnP manager enforces timeouts on driver IRP handling. If a driver hangs while processing a start, stop, or remove request, this bug check fires after the watchdog expires.

The minidump identifies the unresponsive driver. Updating or replacing it resolves the crash.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode with Networking.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Test with minimal peripherals
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect docks, hubs, and external devices; reconnect one at a time to isolate.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: If updates do not help and the system crashes only with a specific dock or hub, replace that accessory.

faq.q: Is this the same as DPC_WATCHDOG?
faq.a: No; DPC_WATCHDOG timeouts are for DPCs, not PnP IRPs.

title: Too Many Dirty Mapped Pages
shortDescription: The memory manager could not flush dirty mapped pages fast enough, congesting the system.
fullDescription:
This bug check indicates the modified-page writer could not keep up with dirty mapped pages, usually because the underlying disk is slow, stalled, or failing. It can also be triggered by a filter driver holding up write I/O.

Check disk health and review any backup or encryption drivers that intercept writes.
symptoms: System becomes very sluggish before crash

fixSteps.title: Check disk SMART and speed
fixSteps.instruction: Run CrystalDiskInfo and CrystalDiskMark; replace disk if sequential writes are abnormally low or SMART flags errors.

fixSteps.title: Disable suspect filter drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Temporarily uninstall antivirus and backup agents, then test stability.

fixSteps.title: Increase pagefile size
fixSteps.instruction: System Properties > Advanced > Performance > Settings > Advanced > Virtual Memory. Set initial and max to 1.5x and 3x RAM.

fixSteps.title: Check disk integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: chkdsk C: /f /r. Allow the scan to run on next reboot.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If the disk is failing, a professional can clone it to a healthy drive before data is lost.

faq.a: Usually no. This is about write I/O, not total memory.

title: Insufficient RAM to Start Windows
shortDescription: Windows does not have enough physical memory to initialize.
fullDescription:
This bug check is rare on modern PCs and means Windows detected less usable RAM than its minimum requirement. Causes include a dislodged memory module, BIOS memory-remapping issues, or badly configured motherboard DIMM slots.

Reseating RAM and clearing CMOS usually restores operation.
symptoms: BIOS shows less RAM than installed

fixSteps.title: Reseat RAM modules
fixSteps.instruction: Power off, unplug, open the case, and remove/reinsert each DIMM firmly into its slot.

fixSteps.title: Test modules individually
fixSteps.instruction: Boot with one DIMM at a time in the primary slot to identify faulty modules.

fixSteps.title: Clear CMOS
fixSteps.instruction: Remove CMOS battery for 30 seconds or use the clear-CMOS jumper.

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS
fixSteps.instruction: Flash the latest firmware supporting your memory.

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

whenToCallPro: If a DIMM slot is confirmed bad, motherboard replacement is often the only fix.

faq.q: Why now after years of use?
faq.a: DIMM contacts can oxidize; a reseat often fixes the issue without buying RAM.

title: Recursive Non-Maskable Interrupt
shortDescription: A non-maskable interrupt occurred while an NMI was already being serviced.
fullDescription:
This rare bug check indicates the CPU received a second NMI while handling the first. NMIs indicate serious hardware events; recursion usually means the NMI source cannot be cleared or the hardware is severely faulting.

It often accompanies failing ECC RAM on server hardware, a faulty PCIe device, or a bad PSU.
symptoms: Hardware errors in Event Viewer WHEA source

fixSteps.title: Test RAM
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe and select Restart now. For deeper testing boot MemTest86 from USB and run at least two full passes.

fixSteps.title: Remove non-essential PCIe cards
fixSteps.instruction: Power down and pull GPUs, HBAs, and NICs one at a time; test after each.

fixSteps.title: Test with known-good PSU
fixSteps.instruction: Swap in a tested PSU of equal or higher capacity.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Check BIOS/firmware
fixSteps.instruction: Install the latest motherboard and storage firmware.

whenToCallPro: This bugcheck almost always indicates hardware failure; professional diagnosis with spare parts is usually required.

faq.a: No. Hardware must be identified and replaced.

title: DirectX Graphics Kernel Fatal Error
shortDescription: The DirectX graphics kernel (dxgkrnl.sys) encountered an unrecoverable error.
fullDescription:
This bug check indicates a fatal failure inside Windows' DirectX kernel component, typically caused by a faulty GPU driver, failing graphics hardware, or memory corruption reaching the display driver.

Updating GPU drivers with DDU and testing with the manufacturer's WHQL release resolves most cases.
symptoms: Crashes during games or video playback
Display driver stopped responding prior to crash

fixSteps.title: Reinstall GPU driver with DDU
fixSteps.instruction: Boot to Safe Mode, run Display Driver Uninstaller to remove current drivers, then install the latest WHQL version from the GPU vendor.

fixSteps.title: Revert GPU overclock
fixSteps.instruction: Use MSI Afterburner or similar to reset core/memory clocks to stock.

fixSteps.title: Monitor GPU temperatures
fixSteps.instruction: Use HWInfo64 under load; throttling above 85C indicates cooling problems.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If a stock GPU at safe temps still crashes, the card may be failing and should be bench-tested by a technician.

faq.a: Not necessarily. Clean driver reinstall fixes most cases.
Sometimes; recent drivers occasionally introduce regressions.

title: Internal Error in GPU Memory Manager
shortDescription: The video memory manager encountered an internal error.
fullDescription:
This bug check is reported by the DirectX video memory manager when its internal bookkeeping becomes inconsistent. Causes include faulty GPU drivers, defective GPU memory, or corrupt shaders.

A clean DDU reinstall of the latest GPU driver is the primary fix.

fixSteps.title: Clean-install GPU driver with DDU
fixSteps.instruction: Boot Safe Mode, run DDU, reinstall the latest WHQL driver.

fixSteps.title: Reset VRAM clock
fixSteps.instruction: Return memory clocks to stock using Afterburner.

fixSteps.title: Test VRAM with OCCT or MemtestG80
fixSteps.instruction: Run VRAM memory tests to check for errors.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

whenToCallPro: If VRAM tests fail or artifacts persist at stock clocks, the GPU likely requires replacement.

faq.a: No. VRAM is soldered on the GPU; replacement is the only option.

title: Multiple UNC Provider Error
shortDescription: The Multiple UNC Provider (MUP) encountered an invalid state processing a network redirect.
fullDescription:
MUP routes UNC paths (\\server\share) to the correct network redirector. This bug check indicates MUP or a redirector returned an unexpected status.

Common causes include broken third-party SMB clients, stale cached credentials, or a malfunctioning network filter driver.
symptoms: BSOD MUP_FILE_SYSTEM when accessing network shares

fixSteps.title: Uninstall third-party SMB/VPN clients
fixSteps.instruction: Remove non-essential network tools and test.

fixSteps.title: Clear stored credentials
fixSteps.instruction: Control Panel > Credential Manager > remove stale Windows credentials.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

whenToCallPro: If the crash persists on a corporate domain, involve the system administrator to check server-side SMB health.

faq.a: It can be. Also investigate server-side SMB and authentication.

title: IOMMU Subsystem Internal Error
shortDescription: The IOMMU (DMA remapping) subsystem reported an internal error.
fullDescription:
This bug check is raised when the IOMMU detects an invalid DMA access or its internal structures become inconsistent. It commonly appears on systems with Hyper-V, WSL2, or virtualization-based security (VBS) enabled where devices use DMA remapping.

BIOS updates and chipset driver updates resolve most cases. Disabling VT-d/AMD-Vi in BIOS can confirm IOMMU as the source.

causes.cause: Incompatible PCIe device with DMA remapping

symptoms: Occurs with PCIe passthrough or virtualization workloads

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS/UEFI
fixSteps.instruction: Install the latest motherboard firmware.

fixSteps.title: Update chipset drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Install the latest chipset package from the CPU/mainboard vendor.

fixSteps.title: Temporarily disable VT-d/AMD-Vi
fixSteps.instruction: Test whether disabling IOMMU in BIOS stops the BSOD (note: disables VBS features).

fixSteps.title: Analyze the crash dump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store. Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver or module.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow. Then run: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Reboot when complete.

whenToCallPro: If BIOS and driver updates do not help, a technician should test whether a specific PCIe device is incompatible with DMA remapping.

If you see this in Event Viewer, update the flagged driver or report the dump to the vendor.

The dump identifies the offending driver; update or remove it.

title: CPU Cache Data Coherency Violation

fullDescription:
This bug check indicates the hardware detected that cached data between CPU cores, caches, or memory was inconsistent. It almost always signals a hardware fault — failing CPU, motherboard, or RAM, or instability from overclocking.

Reset all clocks and voltages to stock and test hardware systematically.

fullDescription:
This bug check is raised when the kernel's Power Dependency Coordinator is waiting for a component to respond during a power transition (sleep, hibernate, modern standby) and the component does not reply in time.

It is commonly caused by buggy drivers for storage, network, or Thunderbolt devices that mishandle power transitions. Modern standby (S0ix) systems are especially prone.

System will not resume from modern standby

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, right-click devices with yellow warning icons or recently updated drivers, and select Update Driver. Prioritize chipset, storage, GPU and network drivers from the OEM.

fixSteps.instruction: Install latest firmware, especially for laptops with modern standby.

faq.a: Rarely; it's most common on modern-standby laptops.

title: Worker Thread Returned at Elevated IRQL
shortDescription: A worker thread returned to the thread pool while running at an elevated IRQL.
fullDescription:
Worker threads must return at PASSIVE_LEVEL (IRQL 0). This bug check means a driver raised IRQL inside a work item and forgot to lower it before the callback returned. The thread pool cannot safely reuse the thread at an elevated IRQL, so Windows halts.

The minidump identifies the faulting driver; the vendor must fix the IRQL mismatch.

causes.cause: Kernel driver work-item with IRQL leak

symptoms: Crash under heavy driver callback load
Minidump names a specific non-Microsoft driver

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift while clicking Restart and choose Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings > Safe Mode.

fixSteps.title: Update device drivers

fixSteps.title: Uninstall security software
fixSteps.instruction: Remove third-party antivirus/EDR using the vendor removal tool and test with Windows Defender only.

fixSteps.title: Analyze the dump
fixSteps.instruction: Open the minidump from C:\Windows\Minidump with WinDbg and run !analyze -v to identify the faulting driver.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open admin Command Prompt and run sfc /scannow followed by DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth.

whenToCallPro: If the minidump points to a signed third-party driver you cannot remove, involve the vendor or a Windows specialist.

faq.q: Is this always a driver bug?
faq.a: Yes. Only kernel drivers can raise IRQL; the responsible driver must ship a fix.
Temporarily by removing the faulty driver; long-term requires a vendor update.

title: Driver Used Excessive Page Table Entries
shortDescription: A driver allocated an excessive number of Page Table Entries, exhausting kernel address space.
fullDescription: The DRIVER_USED_EXCESSIVE_PTES bug check indicates that a driver consumed too many PTEs (Page Table Entries), leaving insufficient kernel virtual memory. This is most common on 32-bit systems running workloads that stress the kernel address space, such as imaging, backup, or storage drivers that perform many MDL mappings.

causes.cause: Driver leaking MDLs or page mappings

symptoms: Crashes during heavy disk I/O or imaging tasks
Event Viewer shows Pool Allocation warnings

fixSteps.title: Analyze minidump
fixSteps.instruction: Open C:\Windows\Minidump with WinDbg or BlueScreenView to identify the faulting driver.

fixSteps.title: Update or roll back drivers
fixSteps.instruction: In Device Manager, identify recently changed devices (display, storage, network). Right-click and choose Update Driver or Roll Back Driver.

fixSteps.title: Increase system PTEs
fixSteps.instruction: Add registry DWORD SystemPages under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management to a higher value (e.g., 0xFFFFFFFF).

fixSteps.title: Switch to 64-bit Windows
fixSteps.instruction: On 32-bit systems chronically hitting PTE exhaustion, upgrading to 64-bit Windows is the real fix.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth

whenToCallPro: If you cannot identify the offending driver from the minidump, a professional can use WinDbg to inspect PTE pool usage.

faq.q: Is this error common on modern Windows?
faq.a: No. It is almost exclusive to 32-bit Windows because 64-bit systems have vastly more kernel virtual address space.
Backup, imaging, storage filter, and antivirus drivers that map large amounts of memory are the most common offenders.
Often yes, because vendors patch MDL leaks. Always try driver updates first.

faq.a: Yes. Fingerprint readers, smart card middleware, and SSO plugins frequently trigger Winlogon crashes after updates.
Usually yes, because Winlogon runs before any user session.
Yes. Disabling non-Microsoft startup services narrows down the culprit.

title: Bad System Configuration Information

fixSteps.instruction: chkdsk C: /f /r from Recovery Command Prompt.

fixSteps.title: System Restore
fixSteps.instruction: Pick a restore point from Recovery.

fixSteps.title: In-place upgrade
fixSteps.instruction: If nothing works, boot installation media and choose Upgrade to repair Windows.
