title: Win32k Critical Failure
shortDescription: The Win32k subsystem encountered an unrecoverable error.
fullDescription: Bug check 0x163 indicates the kernel-mode Win32k graphics and window manager subsystem hit a critical fault. Display drivers, GDI exhaustion, and corrupted fonts are common causes.

fixSteps.title: Update GPU driver
fixSteps.instruction: Install latest NVIDIA/AMD/Intel display driver with a clean install.

fixSteps.title: Rebuild font cache
fixSteps.instruction: Stop Windows Font Cache Service, delete %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts\*.dat, restart service.

fixSteps.title: Remove display hooks
fixSteps.instruction: Uninstall tools like DisplayFusion overlays, F.lux, or RivaTuner that hook Win32k.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt and run: sfc /scannow then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth

fixSteps.title: Analyze minidump
fixSteps.instruction: Open C:\Windows\Minidump with WinDbg or BlueScreenView to identify the faulting driver.

whenToCallPro: If updated drivers and font rebuild do not help, professional analysis of the Win32k call stack is recommended.

faq.q: Can a bad font crash Windows?
faq.a: Yes. Corrupted or malformed font files have historically triggered Win32k crashes.
Yes. Display Driver Uninstaller removes driver remnants before a clean reinstall.

title: Cluster CSV ClusSvc Disconnect Watchdog
shortDescription: The Cluster Shared Volumes watchdog detected that the Cluster Service disconnected.
fullDescription: Bug check 0x166 is issued on Windows Server cluster nodes when the CSV driver detects that the Cluster Service is unresponsive. It ensures the node leaves the cluster gracefully to preserve data integrity.
symptoms: BSOD on cluster node with CLUSTER_CSV_CLUSSVC_DISCONNECT_WATCHDOG

fixSteps.title: Check cluster networks
fixSteps.instruction: Validate cluster network latency and heartbeat settings with Test-Cluster.

fixSteps.title: Inspect storage latency
fixSteps.instruction: Review storage latency on CSV volumes using Performance Monitor.

fixSteps.title: Update NIC and storage drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Apply latest vendor drivers for NICs and HBAs.

fixSteps.title: Adjust CSV timeouts
fixSteps.instruction: Modify SameSubnetThreshold, CrossSubnetThreshold with Set-Cluster as appropriate.

fixSteps.title: Microsoft support
fixSteps.instruction: Open a support case for cluster engineering review.

whenToCallPro: Clustering issues benefit from professional engagement, especially in production Hyper-V or SQL Server clusters.

faq.q: Is this only on Windows Server?
faq.a: Yes, it only occurs on Failover Cluster nodes with CSV.
Sometimes, but the root cause (network or storage) should be addressed.
CSV is designed to fail the node rather than risk data loss; other nodes continue serving.

title: NetAdapter Driver Error
shortDescription: A NetAdapter (NDIS) driver encountered a fatal error.
fullDescription: Bug check 0x169 is raised when a NetAdapter-class driver (Wi-Fi, Ethernet, Bluetooth) fails with an unrecoverable error. Common on laptops after Wi-Fi driver updates.

fixSteps.title: Update network driver
fixSteps.instruction: Install the latest Wi-Fi/Ethernet driver from OEM (HP/Dell/Lenovo).

fixSteps.title: Roll back driver
fixSteps.instruction: If the crash started after an update, roll back in Device Manager.

fixSteps.title: Remove VPN filter drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Uninstall recently installed VPN clients (NordVPN, Cisco AnyConnect).

fixSteps.title: Reset network stack
fixSteps.instruction: netsh winsock reset and netsh int ip reset.

fixSteps.title: Analyze minidump
fixSteps.instruction: Open C:\Windows\Minidump with WinDbg or BlueScreenView to identify the faulting driver.

whenToCallPro: If OEM drivers and stack reset fail, hardware replacement via USB Wi-Fi or professional repair may be needed.

faq.a: As a workaround, yes — but updating the driver is the real fix.
It is often older; the OEM website usually has a newer one.
Rarely — software is the common cause.

title: Cluster ClusPort Status I/O Timeout Livedump

fixSteps.instruction: Use PerfMon counters under Cluster CSV Volumes to measure latency.

fixSteps.title: Review storage fabric
fixSteps.instruction: Check SAN/NAS health and switch counters for dropped frames.

fixSteps.title: Update SMB/MPIO drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Apply latest drivers and hotfixes for SMB Direct and MPIO.

fixSteps.title: Review QoS
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure cluster and storage traffic classes are prioritized correctly.

fixSteps.title: Engage Microsoft support
fixSteps.instruction: For persistent issues, open a cluster support case.

whenToCallPro: Cluster I/O timeouts usually require joint engagement with storage vendor and Microsoft support.

title: Legacy Power State Dispatch Failure
shortDescription: The kernel detected an illegal chained dispatch during a power transition.
fullDescription: BSOD 0xB9 CHAINED_DISPATCH is a rare legacy code raised when kernel IRP dispatching chains encounter illegal state transitions, often during sleep/resume. It is usually triggered by outdated power management filter drivers.
symptoms: Event Viewer System log shows BugCheck 1001

fixSteps.title: Boot into Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Hold Shift and click Restart, then choose Troubleshoot > Advanced > Startup Settings > Safe Mode.

fixSteps.title: Update or roll back drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, identify recently updated drivers and roll back or update them.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open elevated Command Prompt, run: sfc /scannow then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth

fixSteps.title: Analyze minidump
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg (Windows SDK) and analyze C:\Windows\Minidump to identify the faulting driver.

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS/UEFI firmware
fixSteps.instruction: Download the latest BIOS from the motherboard vendor and flash it following their procedure.

whenToCallPro: If repeated after driver updates and SFC/DISM, have a pro analyze the minidump to pinpoint the faulting module.

faq.q: Is CHAINED_DISPATCH usually a driver issue?
faq.a: Yes — most cases trace back to a kernel-mode driver defect.
Occasionally. Run Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86 to rule it out.
Only as a last resort after driver updates, SFC/DISM, and hardware checks fail.

title: Kernel DMA Protection Hardware Violation
shortDescription: Kernel DMA Protection blocked a hardware peripheral's DMA access.
fullDescription: BSOD 0x1DC is raised when Kernel DMA Protection detects an external peripheral attempting unauthorized DMA — typically Thunderbolt or USB4 devices that haven't been remapped via IOMMU.
symptoms: Crash when hot-plugging a Thunderbolt device

fixSteps.title: Disconnect suspect peripheral
fixSteps.instruction: Unplug the Thunderbolt/USB4 device that triggered the crash and verify stability.

fixSteps.title: Update peripheral firmware/drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Install the latest vendor driver/firmware which may add proper DMA remapping support.

fixSteps.title: Update system firmware/UEFI
fixSteps.instruction: Flash latest UEFI from the PC vendor which may extend IOMMU coverage.

fixSteps.title: Toggle DMA Protection policy
fixSteps.instruction: In Windows Security > Device Security > Memory Integrity and Kernel DMA Protection, review enterprise policies.

fixSteps.title: Review minidump
fixSteps.instruction: Use WinDbg on C:\Windows\Minidump to confirm the offending device path.

whenToCallPro: If the violation persists after firmware/driver updates, contact the device vendor.

faq.a: Possibly — unknown DMA peripherals can be attacks. Be cautious of untrusted devices.

title: Kernel Auto-Boost Lock Acquired at Raised IRQL
shortDescription: A driver tried to acquire an auto-boost lock while IRQL was above PASSIVE_LEVEL.
fullDescription: This stop indicates a kernel-mode driver attempted to acquire an auto-boost (ERESOURCE) lock while the processor IRQL was elevated. Auto-boost locks require PASSIVE_LEVEL. The bugcheck is most often a third-party filter driver bug introduced in the 2024 quality updates.
symptoms: Crash while gaming or during AV scan

fixSteps.title: Boot to Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Restart holding Shift, Troubleshoot > Advanced > Startup Settings > Safe Mode.

fixSteps.title: Update filter drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Update AV, anti-cheat (BattlEye, Easy Anti-Cheat) and storage filter drivers.

fixSteps.title: Analyze minidump
fixSteps.instruction: Open C:\Windows\Minidump with WinDbg and run !analyze -v.

fixSteps.title: Uninstall suspect driver
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the driver named in the dump via Programs & Features or pnputil.

fixSteps.title: Install latest cumulative update
fixSteps.instruction: Windows Update > Check for updates — install any pending LCU.

whenToCallPro: Contact Microsoft Support or a qualified technician if the issue persists.

title: Kernel Thread Priority Floor Violation
shortDescription: A driver violated a thread priority floor boost contract.
fullDescription: Introduced in recent Windows kernel builds, this bugcheck fires when KeSetPriorityThread or a scheduler helper is called in a way that breaks the auto-boost priority floor. Typically rooted in third-party scheduler-tweak or power-management utilities.

causes.cause: Kernel patching by old security product

fixSteps.title: Remove CPU tuning utilities
fixSteps.instruction: Uninstall Process Lasso, ThrottleStop-style tools or vendor booster apps.

fixSteps.title: Update GPU driver clean
fixSteps.instruction: DDU in Safe Mode, then install the latest WHQL driver.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC/DISM
fixSteps.instruction: sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth.

fixSteps.title: Roll back recent updates
fixSteps.instruction: Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates.

fixSteps.title: Collect dump for MS
fixSteps.instruction: Submit minidump via Feedback Hub if the pattern persists.

whenToCallPro: Contact Microsoft Support or a qualified technician if the issue persists.

title: Lock Leaked on Thread Termination
shortDescription: A thread terminated while still holding a kernel lock.
fullDescription: Indicates a kernel driver terminated a thread without releasing all acquired ERESOURCEs or push locks. This is a driver bug — frequently in storage, network, or file-system filter drivers.

fixSteps.title: Boot Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Diagnose without third-party drivers loaded.

fixSteps.title: Update all filter drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Update AV, VPN, backup agents.

fixSteps.title: Run Driver Verifier
fixSteps.instruction: verifier /standard /all — reproduce then disable.

fixSteps.title: Remove faulting driver
fixSteps.instruction: Based on verifier output, uninstall the culprit.

fixSteps.title: Apply LCU
fixSteps.instruction: Install pending cumulative update.

whenToCallPro: Contact Microsoft Support or a qualified technician if the issue persists.

title: Invalid Kernel Handle Referenced From User Mode

fullDescription: The kernel detected a user-mode process using a handle that was closed or never valid. Often caused by faulty DRM or anti-cheat drivers, or by memory corruption from a bad system service.
symptoms: Application crashes immediately followed by BSOD 0x1E3
Pattern after launching a specific game

fixSteps.title: Update anti-cheat
fixSteps.instruction: Launch the game so its anti-cheat (EAC/BE/Vanguard) updates.

fixSteps.title: Memtest
fixSteps.instruction: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86.

fixSteps.title: SFC/DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Repair system files.

fixSteps.title: Reinstall game
fixSteps.instruction: Uninstall + reinstall the game in case of anti-cheat binary damage.

fixSteps.title: Collect dump
fixSteps.instruction: Attach minidump to a support ticket.

whenToCallPro: Contact Microsoft Support or a qualified technician if the issue persists.

fixSteps.instruction: Install latest firmware from OEM.

fixSteps.instruction: Lower per-host VM count or CPU overcommit.

fixSteps.instruction: Patch the host OS.

fixSteps.instruction: Event Viewer > Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Hypervisor.

title: DirectX Graphics Kernel Livedump

Games crash to desktop with 'graphics driver stopped responding'

fixSteps.title: Submit feedback
fixSteps.instruction: Upload livedump via Feedback Hub.

whenToCallPro: Contact Microsoft Support or a qualified technician if the issue persists.

fixSteps.instruction: Run extended self-test to confirm drive health.

fixSteps.instruction: Reset Winsock catalog.

fixSteps.instruction: Swap SATA cable or NVMe slot.

fixSteps.title: Update controller firmware
fixSteps.instruction: OEM RAID/HBA firmware.

fixSteps.instruction: Run online chkdsk.

fixSteps.title: Replace drive
fixSteps.instruction: If SMART failing, replace ASAP.

title: INVALID_DATA_ACCESS_TRAP
shortDescription: A kernel-mode thread attempted to access an invalid data area, often due to faulty hardware or driver bug.
fullDescription:
INVALID_DATA_ACCESS_TRAP indicates the operating system trapped an invalid data access from a kernel-mode driver or component. This typically happens when a driver passes a malformed pointer or accesses misaligned data structures.

Faulty hardware (especially RAM and motherboard chipsets) and outdated kernel-mode drivers are the most frequent triggers. The bug can also surface when a driver mishandles structured exception handling.
symptoms: Crash during boot or shortly after login

fixSteps.title: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixSteps.instruction: Press Win+R, type mdsched.exe, and choose Restart now and check for problems.

fixSteps.title: Update kernel-mode drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, focus on chipset, storage, and network drivers; install latest from vendor.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC and DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Open admin Command Prompt: sfc /scannow then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth.

fixSteps.title: Test with one RAM stick
fixSteps.instruction: Boot using a single DIMM, swap to other modules to isolate the bad stick.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

faq.a: It can be either; start with a memory test to rule out RAM, then update drivers.

title: INVALID_KERNEL_HANDLE
shortDescription: A kernel-mode component attempted to close a protected or invalid handle.
fullDescription:
INVALID_KERNEL_HANDLE means a driver tried to call NtClose on a handle that was not created by it or that has special protected flags. This is almost always caused by a third-party driver bug.

It can also be triggered by aggressive kernel debuggers or anti-cheat / antivirus drivers that misuse handle tables.

fixSteps.title: Identify recent driver changes
fixSteps.instruction: Open Reliability Monitor (perfmon /rel) and look for newly installed drivers.

fixSteps.title: Roll back the suspect driver
fixSteps.instruction: In Device Manager right-click the device > Properties > Driver tab > Roll Back Driver.

fixSteps.title: Uninstall third-party AV temporarily
fixSteps.instruction: Use the vendor's official removal tool; reboot and test.

fixSteps.title: Analyze minidump with WinDbg
fixSteps.instruction: Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store, open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp and run !analyze -v.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

title: SECURE_FAULT_UNHANDLED
shortDescription: A security-related fault from VBS or HVCI was not handled by the kernel.
fullDescription:
SECURE_FAULT_UNHANDLED appears on systems with Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) or Memory Integrity (HVCI) enabled when the secure kernel raises a fault that the normal kernel cannot resolve.

It is typically caused by an incompatible kernel driver that violates HVCI's code integrity rules.

causes.cause: Driver incompatible with HVCI / Memory Integrity
CPU virtualization extensions disabled in BIOS

symptoms: BSOD shortly after enabling Core Isolation
Random crashes on systems with VBS enabled
Event 219 or 7000 logged in System log

fixSteps.title: Identify the offending driver
fixSteps.instruction: Open Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation > Memory integrity. Windows lists incompatible drivers.

fixSteps.title: Update or remove incompatible drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Visit each vendor's site for HVCI-compatible builds, or uninstall the driver if no longer needed.

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS/UEFI
fixSteps.instruction: Apply the latest motherboard or laptop firmware from the manufacturer.

fixSteps.title: Temporarily disable Memory Integrity
fixSteps.instruction: If the bad driver cannot be replaced, toggle Memory Integrity off until the vendor releases an update.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

title: RESOURCE_MANAGER_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
shortDescription: The Kernel Transaction Manager raised an unhandled exception.
fullDescription:
This stop is produced by the Kernel Transaction Manager (KTM) when a transactional file system or registry operation experiences an exception that no installed component handled.

It is most often triggered by a flaky filter driver (antivirus, backup, or volume snapshot driver).
symptoms: BSOD during file copy or backup
Reliability Monitor shows recent backup software install

fixSteps.title: List installed filter drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Run fltMC.exe in admin Command Prompt to see active filters.

fixSteps.title: Uninstall recently added backup or AV
fixSteps.instruction: Use the vendor removal tool. Reboot and test.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC/DISM
fixSteps.instruction: Repair system files with sfc /scannow then DISM RestoreHealth.

fixSteps.title: Check disk
fixSteps.instruction: chkdsk C: /f /r on the system volume.

This is almost always a driver bug; Microsoft recommends contacting the driver vendor.

fixSteps.instruction: Provide the minidump for analysis.

title: CDFS_FILE_SYSTEM
shortDescription: An error occurred in the CDFS (CD-ROM) file system driver.
fullDescription:
CDFS_FILE_SYSTEM is raised by cdfs.sys when reading an optical disc fails in an unrecoverable way. Although optical media is rare today, the driver still ships with Windows and is loaded for ISO mounts.

Common triggers are scratched discs, dying optical drives, or malformed ISO images.
symptoms: BSOD when inserting a disc or mounting an ISO
Optical drive not recognized after crash

fixSteps.title: Eject the disc and try another
fixSteps.instruction: Use a different known-good disc; if it works, the original was bad.

fixSteps.title: Test ISO integrity
fixSteps.instruction: Verify the ISO checksum with certutil -hashfile file.iso SHA256.

fixSteps.title: Replace optical drive
fixSteps.instruction: Internal drives are inexpensive; external USB drives are simpler to install.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

SECURITY_SYSTEM (stop 0x29) means the LSA (lsass.exe) or Security Reference Monitor failed in kernel mode. Although LSA itself is user-mode, certain audit or kernel callouts can crash the system.

fixSteps.instruction: If C:\Windows\System32\config\RegBack\SECURITY exists, copy it over the live hive (offline).

fixSteps.title: Run offline antivirus scan
fixSteps.instruction: Use Microsoft Defender Offline or Kaspersky Rescue Disk.

fixSteps.title: Roll back recent updates
fixSteps.instruction: wusa /uninstall /kb:KBNUMBER from WinRE.

shortDescription: The IRQL register was found to contain an unexpected value upon return from a function.
fullDescription:
IRQL_UNEXPECTED_VALUE means a kernel function returned with the processor IRQL set to a different value than it had on entry. This is almost always a driver that forgot to release a spin lock or lower IRQL.

Most cases are caused by old SCSI/RAID, sound, or VPN drivers.
symptoms: Crash after VPN connect or audio device init

fixSteps.title: Disconnect VPN and reboot
fixSteps.instruction: Determine if VPN client is the trigger.

fixSteps.title: Update audio and VPN drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Reinstall latest packages from vendor sites.

fixSteps.title: Run Driver Verifier on third-party drivers
fixSteps.instruction: verifier /standard /driver vendor1.sys vendor2.sys.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

title: RAMDISK_BOOTDISK_FAILURE
shortDescription: Windows failed to mount the RAM disk used during boot (Windows To Go or PXE).
fullDescription:
RAMDISK_BOOTDISK_FAILURE happens when Windows boots from a RAM disk image (typically via Windows Deployment Services or Windows To Go) and the image cannot be opened or initialized.

Causes include a corrupted WIM, insufficient host RAM, or a misconfigured WDS server.
symptoms: BSOD during PXE or USB boot
WDS log records image transfer error

fixSteps.title: Re-export the WIM
fixSteps.instruction: Use DISM /Export-Image to create a fresh boot image.

fixSteps.title: Increase RAM on the target host
fixSteps.instruction: PXE boot typically needs ≥ 2 GB free.

fixSteps.title: Validate WDS share permissions
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure SYSTEM and Network Service have read access on the share.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

title: PAGE_FAULT_WITH_INTERRUPTS_OFF
shortDescription: A page fault occurred while interrupts were disabled, an illegal kernel state.
fullDescription:
PAGE_FAULT_WITH_INTERRUPTS_OFF means a kernel-mode component touched paged memory while it had interrupts disabled (cli). Both a page fault and disabled interrupts are illegal together because the page fault handler needs interrupts.

Driver bug is the typical root cause.

fixSteps.title: Update or roll back drivers
fixSteps.instruction: Particularly storage, network, and security drivers.

fixSteps.title: Stress test CPU
fixSteps.instruction: Prime95 small FFT for 30 min; watch for crashes.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

title: SECURITY1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED
shortDescription: Initialization of the security subsystem failed.
fullDescription:
SECURITY1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED is similar to SECURITY_SYSTEM but happens earlier — during the initialization of the Security Reference Monitor.

The most common cause is a missing or corrupted system file (especially ntoskrnl.exe substitutes after a botched in-place upgrade) or a damaged registry hive.

fixSteps.title: Boot from installation media
fixSteps.instruction: Choose Repair your computer > Troubleshoot > Command Prompt.

fixSteps.title: Run startup repair
fixSteps.instruction: Choose Startup Repair from the Advanced Options menu.

fixSteps.title: Restore registry from RegBack
fixSteps.instruction: Copy SECURITY, SYSTEM, SOFTWARE from RegBack folder if available.

fixSteps.title: Perform in-place upgrade
fixSteps.instruction: Run setup.exe from Windows ISO and choose Keep personal files and apps.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

title: CONFIG_INITIALIZATION_FAILED
shortDescription: Windows failed to initialize the configuration manager (registry).
fullDescription:
CONFIG_INITIALIZATION_FAILED appears when the registry cannot allocate the resources it needs at boot time, or when one of the hives is fundamentally damaged.

This is usually a sign of disk corruption or a system that ran out of paged pool during boot due to a misbehaving driver.

causes.cause: Insufficient paged pool early in boot

fixSteps.title: Run chkdsk from WinRE
fixSteps.instruction: chkdsk C: /f /r in repair Command Prompt.

fixSteps.title: Restore registry hives from RegBack
fixSteps.instruction: Copy hives from C:\Windows\System32\config\RegBack.

fixSteps.title: Use System Restore
fixSteps.instruction: Pick a restore point dated before the crashes started.

whenToCallPro: If the BSOD recurs after driver and memory diagnostics, a technician can analyze minidump files with WinDbg to identify the faulting module.

title: PROCESS1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED
shortDescription: Failure to initialize the first user-mode process (smss.exe).
fullDescription:
PROCESS1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED indicates the Session Manager (smss.exe) could not start. The accompanying parameters identify the failure: missing file, access denied, or unsupported binary.

It is often caused by a missing or corrupted file in C:\Windows\System32 (especially after an antivirus quarantined a system file).
symptoms: BSOD with stop 0x6B before user logon

fixSteps.title: Boot WinRE > Command Prompt
fixSteps.instruction: Use the recovery console to inspect C:\Windows\System32.

fixSteps.title: Restore quarantined files
fixSteps.instruction: From AV quarantine (in Safe Mode if needed), restore any system file.

fixSteps.title: Run SFC offline
fixSteps.instruction: sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows.

fixSteps.title: Roll back updates
fixSteps.instruction: wusa /uninstall /kb:NUMBER /quiet /norestart from WinRE.

title: BGI_DETECTED_VIOLATION
shortDescription: Boot Graphics Initialization detected a security violation.
fullDescription:
BGI_DETECTED_VIOLATION is generated when the boot graphics environment (the early splash logic) detects a violation of its expected state. It is usually associated with Secure Boot inconsistencies or rootkits attempting to hijack boot screens.

It also appears after firmware corruption or aggressive theming utilities that patch ntoskrnl.
symptoms: BSOD just after the OEM logo
Secure Boot status shows Off after firmware update

fixSteps.title: Run an offline AV scan
fixSteps.instruction: Microsoft Defender Offline catches most boot rootkits.

fixSteps.title: Remove theming patchers
fixSteps.instruction: Uninstall UltraUXThemePatcher / SecureUxTheme.

fixSteps.title: Re-enable Secure Boot in BIOS
fixSteps.instruction: Reset Secure Boot to Default Keys.

title: END_OF_NT_EVALUATION_PERIOD
shortDescription: The Windows evaluation period has ended.
fullDescription:
END_OF_NT_EVALUATION_PERIOD is unusual: it does not signal a hardware or driver fault but rather that the time-limited Windows evaluation has expired. It is generated by Windows Server evaluation editions and Insider builds with hard expiry dates.

The fix is to activate the OS or upgrade to a fully licensed edition.

causes.cause: System clock incorrectly set in the future

symptoms: Desktop watermark says Test mode or evaluation

fixSteps.title: Check expiry status
fixSteps.instruction: slmgr /xpr at admin Command Prompt.

fixSteps.title: Upgrade to retail
fixSteps.instruction: Use DISM /Online /Set-Edition with the right edition ID and a valid product key.

fixSteps.title: Verify system time
fixSteps.instruction: Settings > Time & Language > Sync now.

title: ACPI_DRIVER_INTERNAL
shortDescription: The ACPI driver detected an internal inconsistency.
fullDescription:
ACPI_DRIVER_INTERNAL is raised by acpi.sys when the OS sees behavior from the system firmware (BIOS/UEFI) that violates the ACPI specification.

It is most common on systems with an old BIOS that has not been updated for a newer Windows version.

causes.cause: Buggy ACPI table after dock connect
Hardware fault on an ACPI-controlled device

symptoms: BSOD on resume from sleep or dock connect
Stop 0xA3 with parameter pointing to ACPI namespace

fixSteps.title: Update BIOS/UEFI
fixSteps.instruction: Download the latest firmware from the OEM site and apply.

fixSteps.title: Disconnect external dock or USB-C hub
fixSteps.instruction: Test without the accessory; replace if it triggers crashes.

fixSteps.title: Disable hybrid sleep
fixSteps.instruction: powercfg /h off and disable sleep/hibernate temporarily.

title: DRIVER_CAUGHT_MODIFYING_FREED_POOL
shortDescription: A driver was caught writing to memory it had already freed.
fullDescription:
DRIVER_CAUGHT_MODIFYING_FREED_POOL is a Driver Verifier-detected bug: the verifier caught a driver writing into a freed pool allocation (use-after-free).

This is purely a driver bug. Disable Driver Verifier if the system has become unbootable, then update or remove the offending driver.
symptoms: BSOD on systems with Driver Verifier active

fixSteps.title: Disable Driver Verifier from Safe Mode
fixSteps.instruction: verifier /reset, then reboot.

fixSteps.title: Identify and uninstall the bad driver
fixSteps.instruction: Use the IMAGE_NAME from the dump to find the vendor; remove or update.

fixSteps.title: Re-enable verifier on remaining drivers only
fixSteps.instruction: verifier /standard /all /except vendor.sys.

title: PAGE_FAULT_IN_FREED_SPECIAL_POOL
shortDescription: A driver accessed memory after it was freed from special pool.
fullDescription:
PAGE_FAULT_IN_FREED_SPECIAL_POOL is another Driver Verifier-detected use-after-free, similar to 0xC6 but with allocations from the special pool. Special pool is typically enabled to catch precisely this class of bugs.

Fix the driver or remove it.
symptoms: Repeated crashes after enabling special pool

fixSteps.title: Identify the driver
fixSteps.instruction: Open the dump in WinDbg; !analyze -v reveals the module.

fixSteps.title: Disable verifier and remove the driver
fixSteps.instruction: verifier /reset and uninstall the offender.

fixSteps.title: Report to vendor
fixSteps.instruction: Provide minidumps and verifier flags so the vendor can patch.

fullDescription:
INSTRUCTION_COHERENCY_EXCEPTION (0x56) is rare and indicates the CPU's instruction cache is inconsistent with memory. Typically a sign of unstable overclocks, marginal power, or a failing CPU.

Reset BIOS overclocks; if defaults still crash, the CPU may need replacement.

fixSteps.instruction: Reset CPU multiplier and voltages.

fixSteps.title: Stress test
fixSteps.instruction: Prime95 1 hour at stock.

fixSteps.title: RMA CPU if persists
fixSteps.instruction: Crashes at stock indicate hardware fault.

fullDescription:
UNSUPPORTED_INSTRUCTION_MODE (0x130) means a thread tried to execute an instruction the current CPU mode does not allow. It points to corrupted thread context, often from RAM faults or stack overruns.

Memory diagnostic and driver checks come first.

fixSteps.instruction: MemTest86 full pass.

fixSteps.instruction: Storage, network, GPU.

fixSteps.instruction: Open Device Manager, update the suspect driver (graphics, storage, network) or roll back if the crash started after an update.

fixSteps.instruction: In an elevated Command Prompt run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then run Windows Memory Diagnostic (mdsched.exe).

fixSteps.instruction: Open C:\Windows\Minidump\*.dmp in WinDbg or BlueScreenView to identify the failing module, then update or uninstall that driver.
